extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, research-integrity professionals, and science journalists following retractions and misconduct
extracted.subtask_description: News/blog coverage summarizing cases and standards that trigger retraction, expressions of concern, and institutional or funder sanctions — with examples from China-related cases. Useful for people tracking research integrity, journal practice, and misconduct consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of donor consent and organ source
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies of organ transplants that “didn’t report whether the sources gave their consent for donation, nor assurances the organs involved did not come from executed prisoners.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BMJ Open analysis found more than 400 such studies; failure to report donor consent or to assure organs were not from executed prisoners is presented as a substantive ethical failing that can prompt flags, expressions of concern, and calls for retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with international ethical standards in transplantation research
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals must comply with international ethical standards to ensure organ donors provide consent for transplantation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted as a “mass failure of English language medical journals to comply with international ethical standards” — journals are expected to require documentation/assurances about consent and source of organs before publishing transplantation research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of investigative analyses as grounds for retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Retractions or flags may be prompted by external investigative studies (e.g., the Rogers paper) that identify systemic ethical problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece notes that 13 retractions this year directly cite the Rogers paper, illustrating that rigorous external analyses can catalyze journal corrective actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of concern versus retraction practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals may issue expressions of concern or retract papers; many flagged papers remain as expressions of concern rather than retracted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Of a set of 445 papers identified, only 44 had been retracted to date while at least 17 remained marked with expressions of concern — indicating variability and delay in journal responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper mill activity and plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Engagement with paper mills and instances of plagiarism are identified as misconduct driving sanctions and retractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NSFC investigations listed paper mill activity and plagiarism among violations and enumerated specific papers and grant applications tied to these behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Falsified or fabricated research
rubrics_metrics.description: Potentially falsified research (data or results manufactured or altered) is a ground for publisher investigations and retractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Frontiers retracted at least a dozen papers after an “extensive internal investigation” into potentially falsified research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image manipulation and misused images
rubrics_metrics.description: Manipulated or misused images in articles are cited as reasons for retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A cancer journal retracted multiple articles after concluding they contained manipulated or misused images; the report references prior large-scale cleanses for image-related problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fake peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrupt peer-review processes (fake peer review) are grounds for mass retractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tumor Biology’s prior forced retraction of 107 papers is attributed to corruption by fake peer review, demonstrating this as a systemic failure mode journals must police.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplicate publication / redundant publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing the same data in multiple journals (duplicate publication) is misconduct that can lead to retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an anesthesiologist received a fourth retraction for publishing the same data in two Springer Nature journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buying and selling authorship; authorship misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Buying and selling authorship is named among misconduct practices that invoke sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NSFC reports and other cases list buying and selling authorship alongside plagiarism and image manipulation as sanctionable behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional and funder sanctions and penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions and funding agencies may impose sanctions ranging from bans on applying for funding or serving as reviewers to revoking funds and requiring returns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NSFC penalties included bans on applying for funding or serving as a reviewer, revoking research funding (including returning dispersed funds), and other restrictions for specified periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration and severity of sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions often have defined durations and severity levels (e.g., 3–7 year bans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In many NSFC cases, restrictions on applying for funding were for three to seven years; penalties vary by offense and may include funding revocation and professional restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree revocation and employment consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Universities may revoke degrees and terminate employment for researchers who used paper mills or committed severe misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include revocation of a medical degree for using a paper mill to write a dissertation and firing or dismissal tied to suspected coercion or misconduct around publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher-led internal investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers may conduct internal investigations that result in multiple retractions once potential misconduct or falsification is identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frontiers’ internal investigation led to a wave of retractions; such publisher reviews are a recognized mechanism for detecting and correcting the literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author disputes and contested reasons for retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may contest or attribute retractions to external pressures (e.g., censorship) rather than admitted misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases described where authors blamed censorship for a retraction — indicating that retraction reasons can be disputed and that notices and context matter for interpreting retraction causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of retractions (citations and literature record)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retractions affect the scientific record but some retracted or suspect papers remain cited or in databases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a retracted JCMC paper had been cited four times; the broader topic notes slow clearing of the literature despite evidence of widespread problems.
